name: LearnPack Pedagogical Rubric
scope: For a subject-matter expert judging a deployed LearnPack course by taking it as a learner would, end to end. Twelve statements; each answered as agreement on the same five points. What it produces is the reference automated assessors are compared against — not a published verdict on a course, and not a score anyone reports.
evaluatorMaterials: the deployed course, all lessons, taken as a learner would take it

items.prompt: The course's objectives are phrased with observable action verbs.
items.guidance: Agree if every objective names an observable action a learner could be watched performing — solve, classify, build, debug. Disagree if objectives only list topics the course will cover, or name internal states you cannot observe from outside, such as 'understand', 'learn about' or 'get familiar with'.

items.prompt: The course starts at a point reachable from the audience's declared background.
items.guidance: Agree if what the course assumes the audience already knows is either named for them or fair to assume of that audience. Disagree if it demands knowledge that audience would not have, or leans on ideas it never names and that audience would not bring.

items.prompt: Every declared objective is developed by some part of the content.
items.guidance: Agree if every declared objective has a part of the content that actually develops it, not merely a mention. Disagree if any objective is only named in passing, with no part of the content actually developing it.

items.prompt: Each declared objective is measured by at least one of the assessment tasks the course offers.
items.guidance: Agree if every declared objective has a task that would show whether a learner can actually do it. Disagree if there are no tasks, if the tasks check something other than what the objectives declare, or if they only ask the learner to recall what was said.

items.prompt: New instructional material is motivated by a real problem or task rather than introduced as abstract exposition.
items.guidance: Agree if new material is almost always preceded by a concrete, real problem or task that motivates it. Disagree if lessons introduce it as abstract exposition — definitions and theory first — with the reason to care, if it comes at all, arriving afterwards.

items.prompt: New skills are demonstrated with worked examples before practice.
items.guidance: Agree if every skill the course teaches is shown worked through with a concrete example before the learner practices it. Disagree if the course describes how something is done without ever showing it done, or jumps straight from description to practice.

items.prompt: Lessons connect new material to what the learner already knows.
items.guidance: Agree if new material is tied to prior knowledge, or to everyday experience this audience would have. Disagree if new material arrives with no bridge from anything the learner brings, as self-contained blocks of information.

items.prompt: Lessons follow an order where each builds on the previous ones.
items.guidance: Agree if the order the lessons follow is doing work — each one builds on, or needs, the ones before it. Disagree if the lessons could be shuffled with little loss, because each stands on its own.

items.prompt: Earlier concepts are integrated into what comes later, not repeated in isolation.
items.guidance: Agree if later material draws on earlier concepts to build something new, not just recap them. Disagree if an earlier concept's later appearances are disconnected from what surrounds them — restated on their own, with nothing new built from them.

items.prompt: The course makes the connections between its lessons and ideas explicit, rather than leaving the learner to infer them.
items.guidance: This is not about whether the sequence is coherent, but about whether the course says so. Agree if the course tells the learner how its parts relate: why this comes after that, what an idea builds on. Disagree if lessons are presented one after another and the learner has to work out for themselves how they relate.

items.prompt: Ideas the course builds on are introduced before they are needed.
items.guidance: Agree if every idea a lesson depends on was introduced earlier in the course, or is genuinely part of the background this course is written for. Disagree if lessons depend on ideas that were never introduced and that this audience would not be expected to bring.

items.prompt: The course grows more demanding at a pace a learner who has kept up could still follow.
items.guidance: Agree if the course gets steadily more demanding and each step is reachable from the one before. Disagree if it stays flat throughout, or if at least one lesson runs far ahead of the rest of the course.

frameworks.citation: Merrill, M. D. (2002). First Principles of Instruction. ETR&D, 50(3), 43-59.
Biggs, J. (1996). Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32, 347-364.
Anderson & Krathwohl (2001); Krathwohl (2002), Theory Into Practice, 41(4), 212-218.
Biggs & Collis (1982). Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy.
Schmidt, Wang & McKnight (2005); Schmidt, Houang & Cogan (2002). Curriculum coherence.
Duschl, Maeng & Sezen (2011). Learning progressions and teaching sequences.
